Your work will define how the world transacts.Speed and craft compoundOur goal is to get faster as Stripe grows. We also revere craftsmanship and obsess over every detail. The tension between those two operating principles – speed and craft – defines how we work.Better defaults existWe don't assume the best way to do something is the way it's always been done. We rethink from first principles how financial services should work, and welcome new ideas from every corner of the company.Built for the bestWe power the world's most ambitious companies because we're obsessed with their success, rigorous about the details, creative in our approach, and always moving with urgency.We're building the economic infrastructure for AIAI is replatforming the global economy. Stripe is building infrastructure to make it possible, including real-time agent micropayments, protocols that let software transact autonomously and fraud prevention for a new generation of threats. These are just some of the challenges you'll be working on.Around 1.7% of global GDP runs on Stripe.Behind every transaction is something someone here built.Solve the problems that matter at scaleStripe is focused on improving the conditions for economic growth and prosperity. We're seeing less growth in the 21st century than we did in the 20th. In rich countries, slower growth corresponds to less innovation and more fractious politics. In poor countries, it means sustained material deprivation. In either case, we need to do better, and we want your help. We're at the centre of this, and we think the best work is still in front of us. hiring_pages.text: OpportunityCompatibilityEmerging talentOpen rolesOpen rolesCompatibilityWorking at Stripe is not for everyoneNot everyone finds success at Stripe. Those who do tend to share a few things in common.The right people don't always think they're rightSuccessful Stripes are rigorous thinkers who appreciate that things worth doing are rarely simple. We want people who are not afraid to be wrong, who can enthusiastically back proposals they initially opposed and who know how to support decisions with numbers and narrative. We operate in situations of substantial uncertainty and cannot afford either timidity or recklessness. The global financial system can seem like a mystifying domain. It isn't. It's made of people and computers, like many other systems you've worked on. Most Stripes don't come from finance, and they've thrived by bringing fresh perspectives. We want generalists who can parachute anywhere into our operations, learn a new field quickly and execute competently beyond their formal remit. We know that we can't be successful without nurturing the careers of both generalists and experts. People who thrive in high-conflict work environments often do not enjoy the experience here. We try to embrace kindness while still encouraging Stripes to take measured risks and act boldly, even in the absence of consensus.Who is Stripe for?Ambitious buildersWe're building solutions without clear precedent, solving problems with far-reaching consequences. The people here find that energising, preferring the joy of discovery to the comfort of certainty.Adaptable problem solversAI is changing how the global economy works, how our customers work and how Stripes work. The people who thrive here adapt quickly and treat obstacles as opportunities.Rigorous thinkersWe argue from first principles, question assumptions, and don't stop at "good enough."The most successful Stripes are the people who have the intellectual horsepower, the curiosity to learn a very complicated business and the humility to get up every day and realise there's a huge amount of things they don't know.Conor McNamaraHead of EMEAWhat all Stripes have in commonWe're dedicated to our work and optimistic about the world. We believe entrepreneurship and free markets do good, and building what supports them matters. If that's you, read on.Motivated by our missionStripe is on a mission to grow the GDP of the internet.Ask yourself:​Do I see free markets and entrepreneurship as powerful forces for advancing progress?​Does enabling entrepreneurship and helping to unlock the internet economy's full potential seem like a compelling use of my time and talents?Embody our operating principles“Users first” is a cornerstone principle. Our users trust us to provide an essential service, and it's a heavy responsibility that we take very seriously.Ask yourself:​Am I motivated to move mountains to protect and support businesses that depend on Stripe?​Am I driven to overcome obstacles and take on big things to drive progress, or do I feel overwhelmed by the sheer scale and breadth of sometimes nebulous opportunities?Energised by changeThe pace of change at Stripe and in the broader economy is accelerating. You'll work outside your domain, take on problems that didn't exist a year ago and be expected to adapt as quickly as the world does.Ask yourself:​Do I see a fast-moving environment as an opportunity rather than an obstacle?​Am I comfortable taking on problems outside my domain or experience?Collaborative, multidisciplinary workBuilding programmable financial infrastructure from first principles is inherently complex. Well-crafted work indicates care for the user, and beautiful work indicates care for the world.Move with urgency and focusWe move with speed on what matters most and take the time to invest in what will make us faster tomorrow. Whereas many companies get slower until they're eventually mired in mediocrity, we aspire to become the world's fastest company.Collaborate egolesslyWe work as one team: no fiefdoms, no hoarding information, no "not my problem." We question assumptions, debate energetically and abandon ideas when better ones emerge. We're generous with credit and stingy with blame. We learn from mistakes together.Stay curiousStripe is an applied exercise in learning about how businesses tick and how the world works. Since the details and possibilities are infinite, we are always seeking to learn. We're energised by the unfamiliar, preferring the joy of discovery to the comfort of certainty.Obsess over talentIt's every Stripe's responsibility to help hire the best and to push for excellence everywhere. Managers must relentlessly uphold our high talent bar, lead their teams with clarity and context, foster development and ultimately support Stripes in accomplishing the best work of their careers.Our cultureLike all great workplaces, Stripe has its own working culture, with norms that can surprise, delight and occasionally perplex.Friday FiresideFriday Fireside is a weekly Stripe-wide forum hosted by Patrick and John. initial_questions.prompt: How do you approach mentoring junior engineers and conducting code reviews? Provide an example of how you improved a team's engineering practices.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how you would design a TypeScript/Node.js service to handle high concurrency and CPU-bound tasks without blocking the event loop. Discuss worker threads, clustering, and async patterns.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover event loop mechanics, offloading CPU-bound work to worker threads or separate processes, using clusters for multi-core, and async/await best practices. Mention monitoring and profiling.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the key differences between TypeScript and JavaScript in a large backend codebase? How do you enforce type safety and manage dependencies?

initial_questions.prompt: How would you optimize a slow PostgreSQL query that involves multiple joins and aggregations on large tables? Walk through your diagnostic process and potential solutions.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how you would design a schema for a financial ledger system in PostgreSQL, ensuring ACID compliance and auditability. Discuss transaction isolation levels and locking.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a distributed system for processing payments that must be highly available and partition-tolerant. Discuss consistency models, CAP theorem trade-offs, and failure handling.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should choose appropriate consistency (e.g., eventual for some parts, strong for financial transactions), discuss idempotency, retries, circuit breakers, and distributed transactions (Saga pattern).

initial_questions.prompt: How do you handle distributed tracing and debugging in a microservices architecture? Describe tools and patterns you have used.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect mention of OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, correlation IDs, logging aggregation, and service meshes. Discuss challenges like clock skew and data volume.

initial_questions.prompt: Compare REST and event-driven architectures for a payment processing system. When would you choose one over the other, and how would you combine them?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss synchronous vs asynchronous communication, coupling, scalability, and reliability. Mention REST for client-facing APIs and events for internal workflows, with idempotency and exactly-once semantics.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you ensure idempotency and exactly-once processing in event-driven systems? Provide examples from your experience.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect techniques like idempotency keys, deduplication, transactional outbox, and at-least-once with consumer dedup. Discuss trade-offs and failure scenarios.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe your experience with AWS services for building scalable backend systems. Which services have you used, and how did you handle security, cost, and reliability?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should mention compute (EC2, Lambda, ECS/EKS), storage (S3, RDS), messaging (SQS, SNS), and IAM. Discuss VPC, auto-scaling, cost optimization, and disaster recovery.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you design a multi-region, fault-tolerant architecture on AWS for a financial application? Discuss data replication, failover, and compliance.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect use of Route 53, global tables, cross-region replication, and backup strategies. Mention compliance (PCI DSS) and latency considerations.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the key considerations when integrating with payment gateways (e.g., Stripe, PayPal)? How do you handle reconciliation and error scenarios?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss API integration, webhooks, idempotency, retries, and reconciliation processes. Mention PCI compliance and tokenization.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how you would design a double-entry bookkeeping system for a financial application. What are the critical requirements?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect immutable ledgers, balanced transactions, audit trails, and consistency checks. Discuss handling of currency and rounding.

initial_questions.prompt: How does Kafka ensure message ordering and durability? How would you use Kafka in a payment processing pipeline?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should explain partitions, replication, acks, and consumer groups. Discuss exactly-once semantics, idempotent producers, and transactional messaging.

initial_questions.prompt: What are common pitfalls when using Kafka in production, and how do you monitor and mitigate them?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect issues like consumer lag, rebalancing, message duplication, and broker failures. Mention monitoring tools (e.g., Burrow, Prometheus) and best practices.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe how you would deploy a Node.js application on Kubernetes. What are the key considerations for configuration, scaling, and health checks?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover Dockerization, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps/Secrets, liveness/readiness probes, and HPA. Discuss logging and monitoring.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you manage secrets and sensitive data in Kubernetes? Discuss best practices and tools.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect use of Kubernetes Secrets, external secret managers (e.g., Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), encryption at rest, and RBAC. Mention avoiding hardcoding and using service accounts.

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 5+ years of backend engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight a progression of backend roles, key projects (e.g., scaling services, database optimization), and measurable impacts like reduced latency or increased throughput. Emphasize sustained responsibility for production systems.

flashcards.front: What are key TypeScript/Node.js concepts for backend interviews?
flashcards.back: Event loop, async/await, streams, error handling, module system, and performance profiling. Be ready to discuss building scalable APIs, using frameworks like Express/NestJS, and type safety in large codebases.

flashcards.front: How do you optimize PostgreSQL performance?
flashcards.back: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, proper indexing (B-tree, GIN, etc.), query rewriting, connection pooling, partitioning, and caching. Discuss trade-offs between normalization and denormalization, and monitoring with pg_stat_statements.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations when designing distributed systems?
flashcards.back: CAP theorem, consistency models, fault tolerance, partitioning, replication, consensus (Raft/Paxos), and idempotency. Discuss trade-offs like latency vs consistency and how to handle partial failures.

flashcards.front: How do REST APIs and event-driven systems differ, and when to use each?
flashcards.back: REST is synchronous request-response, good for CRUD and immediate feedback. Event-driven is asynchronous, decoupled, good for scalability and real-time processing. Often combined: REST for commands, events for propagation.

flashcards.front: What AWS services are essential for backend engineers?
flashcards.back: EC2, Lambda, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, ECS/EKS, CloudWatch. Understand IAM, VPC, and cost optimization. Be ready to design a fault-tolerant architecture using these.

flashcards.front: How have you mentored engineers?
flashcards.back: Provide examples: code reviews, pair programming, design doc feedback, onboarding buddies, and creating learning resources. Emphasize tailored guidance, fostering independence, and tracking growth.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure strong communication and collaboration in engineering?
flashcards.back: Use clear written docs (RFCs, design docs), active listening, constructive feedback, and cross-functional collaboration. Example: leading a project with product and QA, resolving conflicts, and aligning stakeholders.

flashcards.front: What challenges are unique to payments/financial systems?
flashcards.back: Idempotency, exactly-once processing, audit trails, PCI compliance, fraud detection, and reconciliation. Discuss handling money as integers, double-entry ledgers, and dealing with distributed transactions (Sagas).

flashcards.front: How does Kafka work and when would you use it?
flashcards.back: Kafka is a distributed log with topics, partitions, producers, consumers, and consumer groups. Use for high-throughput, fault-tolerant event streaming, log aggregation, and decoupling. Discuss offset management, rebalancing, and exactly-once semantics.

flashcards.front: What are key Kubernetes concepts for backend engineers?
flashcards.back: Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and autoscaling. Understand rolling updates, resource limits, liveness/readiness probes, and debugging with kubectl. Discuss when to use K8s vs simpler solutions.

questions.answer_outline: Situation: Outline the team composition and challenges. Task: Your goal to mentor effectively. Action: Explain how you tailored your approach (e.g., individualized plans, different communication methods). Result: Highlight each engineer's growth and overall team success.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a time when you had to collaborate with a difficult stakeholder or team member to achieve a common goal. How did you handle the communication?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: Describe the difficult person and the project. Task: Your role in collaboration. Action: Explain how you communicated (e.g., active listening, finding common ground, adjusting style). Result: Outcome of the collaboration and any lessons learned.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when you had to explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical audience. How did you ensure understanding?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: Context of the audience and topic. Task: Your goal to communicate clearly. Action: Describe techniques used (e.g., analogies, visuals, avoiding jargon). Result: How the audience responded and the impact.

questions.prompt: Stripe's mission is to increase the GDP of the internet by building financial infrastructure. Describe a backend system you designed and built that handled significant scale or complexity. What was your specific role, and how did you ensure reliability and correctness in the face of failures?
questions.answer_outline: Look for 5+ years of backend experience, depth in TypeScript/Node.js and PostgreSQL, and evidence of designing distributed systems. Strong answers will highlight ownership, trade-offs, failure handling, and measurable impact. They should connect their experience to Stripe's need for reliable financial infrastructure.

questions.prompt: Stripe's products rely heavily on APIs and event-driven architectures to move money and data reliably. Can you walk us through a system you built that used REST APIs and event-driven patterns? How did you handle idempotency, ordering, and delivery guarantees, and what cloud services did you leverage?
questions.answer_outline: Expect experience with REST and event-driven systems, AWS or similar cloud, and ideally Kafka. Look for concrete examples of designing for idempotency, at-least-once delivery, and ordering. Strong candidates will discuss trade-offs and how they ensured data consistency.

questions.prompt: Mentoring and collaboration are core to how we work at Stripe. Tell us about a time you mentored a less experienced engineer or led a cross-functional project. How did you approach knowledge sharing and ensure alignment across teams?
questions.answer_outline: Seek evidence of mentoring, strong communication, and collaboration. Look for specific examples of guiding others, giving feedback, and working across teams. Strong answers will show empathy, clarity, and a focus on team outcomes.

questions.prompt: Stripe operates in the payments domain, where correctness and consistency are critical. If you have experience with payments or financial systems, describe a challenge you faced related to data consistency or transaction integrity. If not, how would you approach learning the domain and ensuring correctness in a system like ours?
questions.answer_outline: For those with payments experience, look for deep understanding of ACID, isolation levels, and financial correctness. For others, assess their ability to learn quickly and apply distributed systems principles to a new domain. Strong answers will emphasize testing, monitoring, and careful design.

questions.prompt: Stripe's infrastructure runs on cloud platforms and often uses Kubernetes for orchestration. Can you describe your experience with Kubernetes or similar container orchestration? How have you used it to deploy and manage services, and what challenges did you encounter?
questions.answer_outline: Look for hands-on experience with Kubernetes, including deployments, scaling, and troubleshooting. Strong answers will discuss operational challenges, monitoring, and how they ensured reliability. If no Kubernetes, assess experience with other orchestration or cloud-native tools.

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 5+ years of backend engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight a progression of backend roles, key projects (e.g., scaling services, database optimization), and measurable impacts like reduced latency or increased throughput. Emphasize sustained responsibility for production systems.

flashcards.front: What are key TypeScript/Node.js concepts for backend interviews?
flashcards.back: Event loop, async/await, streams, error handling, module system, and performance profiling. Be ready to discuss building scalable APIs, using frameworks like Express/NestJS, and type safety in large codebases.

flashcards.front: How do you optimize PostgreSQL performance?
flashcards.back: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, proper indexing (B-tree, GIN, etc.), query rewriting, connection pooling, partitioning, and caching. Discuss trade-offs between normalization and denormalization, and monitoring with pg_stat_statements.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations when designing distributed systems?
flashcards.back: CAP theorem, consistency models, fault tolerance, partitioning, replication, consensus (Raft/Paxos), and idempotency. Discuss trade-offs like latency vs consistency and how to handle partial failures.

flashcards.front: How do REST APIs and event-driven systems differ, and when to use each?
flashcards.back: REST is synchronous request-response, good for CRUD and immediate feedback. Event-driven is asynchronous, decoupled, good for scalability and real-time processing. Often combined: REST for commands, events for propagation.

flashcards.front: What AWS services are essential for backend engineers?
flashcards.back: EC2, Lambda, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, ECS/EKS, CloudWatch. Understand IAM, VPC, and cost optimization. Be ready to design a fault-tolerant architecture using these.

flashcards.front: How have you mentored engineers?
flashcards.back: Provide examples: code reviews, pair programming, design doc feedback, onboarding buddies, and creating learning resources. Emphasize tailored guidance, fostering independence, and tracking growth.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure strong communication and collaboration in engineering?
flashcards.back: Use clear written docs (RFCs, design docs), active listening, constructive feedback, and cross-functional collaboration. Example: leading a project with product and QA, resolving conflicts, and aligning stakeholders.

flashcards.front: What challenges are unique to payments/financial systems?
flashcards.back: Idempotency, exactly-once processing, audit trails, PCI compliance, fraud detection, and reconciliation. Discuss handling money as integers, double-entry ledgers, and dealing with distributed transactions (Sagas).

flashcards.front: How does Kafka work and when would you use it?
flashcards.back: Kafka is a distributed log with topics, partitions, producers, consumers, and consumer groups. Use for high-throughput, fault-tolerant event streaming, log aggregation, and decoupling. Discuss offset management, rebalancing, and exactly-once semantics.

flashcards.front: What are key Kubernetes concepts for backend engineers?
flashcards.back: Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and autoscaling. Understand rolling updates, resource limits, liveness/readiness probes, and debugging with kubectl. Discuss when to use K8s vs simpler solutions.

initial_questions.prompt: You are reviewing a Ruby on Rails service that handles user authentication and order processing. The service has grown organically, and you notice that the User model contains methods for sending emails, calculating discounts, and generating PDF invoices. How would you refactor this to adhere to SOLID principles and improve maintainability? Provide specific code organization strategies.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Identify violations of Single Responsibility Principle: User model has multiple reasons to change. Suggest extracting concerns into service objects (e.g., EmailService, DiscountCalculator, InvoiceGenerator) and using composition. Discuss benefits: testability, separation of concerns, easier future changes. Mention potential use of ActiveSupport::Concern for shared behavior but caution against overuse. Emphasize dependency injection for services.

initial_questions.prompt: In a Node.js backend, you need to implement a feature that processes a large CSV file (several GB) and inserts records into a database. The current implementation reads the entire file into memory, causing out-of-memory errors. How would you redesign this to handle the file efficiently? Discuss streams, backpressure, and error handling.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Use Node.js streams: create a readable stream from the file, pipe through a CSV parser (e.g., csv-parser), and process rows in chunks. Implement backpressure by pausing the stream when database writes are slow. Use a write stream or batch inserts to the database. Handle errors with try/catch and stream error events. Consider using worker threads for CPU-intensive parsing. Mention monitoring memory usage and using tools like clinic.js.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a REST API for a simple blog platform. The API should allow creating, reading, updating, and deleting posts, and also retrieving comments for a post. Specify the endpoints, HTTP methods, status codes, and request/response formats. How would you handle pagination for the list of posts?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Endpoints: GET /posts (list, with pagination), POST /posts (create), GET /posts/{id} (read), PUT /posts/{id} (update), DELETE /posts/{id} (delete), GET /posts/{id}/comments (list comments). Use appropriate status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found. Request/response in JSON. Pagination: use query parameters like ?page=1&limit=10, return metadata (total count, links). Discuss HATEOAS optionally. Mention versioning via URL or headers.

initial_questions.prompt: You are building a REST API that needs to support partial updates and optimistic concurrency control. How would you design the API to handle PATCH requests and prevent lost updates? Discuss the use of ETags, If-Match headers, and how to handle conflicts.
initial_questions.answer_outline: For partial updates, use PATCH with JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) or JSON Patch (RFC 6902). For optimistic concurrency, include an ETag header in GET responses (e.g., based on resource version or last modified timestamp). Clients send If-Match header with the ETag when updating. Server checks if ETag matches current version; if not, return 412 Precondition Failed. On conflict, return 409 Conflict with details. Discuss idempotency and retry strategies.

flashcards.front: What does '3+ years of backend development experience' typically entail?
flashcards.back: It means you have at least three years of professional experience building and maintaining server-side applications, including designing APIs, working with databases, and deploying to production.

flashcards.front: Which languages are commonly used for backend development in this context?
flashcards.back: Ruby (especially with Rails) and Node.js are explicitly mentioned, but similar backend languages like Python, Java, or Go may also qualify.

flashcards.front: What is a REST API and why is it important?
flashcards.back: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to perform CRUD operations on resources, enabling stateless, scalable communication between clients and servers.

flashcards.front: What are key concepts in SQL and relational databases?
flashcards.back: Key concepts include tables, rows, columns, primary keys, foreign keys, indexes, joins, transactions, ACID properties, and normalization. Proficiency in writing complex queries and optimizing performance is essential.

flashcards.front: What are distributed systems and why are they used?
flashcards.back: Distributed systems are collections of independent computers that appear as a single coherent system to users. They are used for scalability, fault tolerance, and high availability, but introduce challenges like network latency, consistency, and partitioning.

flashcards.front: What considerations are important for high-traffic applications?
flashcards.back: High-traffic applications require scalability (horizontal/vertical), caching, load balancing, database sharding/replication, asynchronous processing, and monitoring to handle large volumes of requests without downtime.

flashcards.front: How can you demonstrate strong problem-solving skills in an interview?
flashcards.back: By walking through your thought process, breaking down complex problems, considering trade-offs, and describing how you've debugged and resolved issues in past projects.

flashcards.front: What does effective collaboration with product and engineering teams involve?
flashcards.back: It involves clear communication, understanding business requirements, providing technical feasibility feedback, participating in agile ceremonies, and aligning engineering efforts with product goals.

flashcards.front: What are common e-commerce backend challenges?
flashcards.back: Challenges include inventory management, payment processing, order fulfillment, scalability during peak traffic, security (PCI compliance), and integrating with third-party services.

flashcards.front: What is GraphQL and how does it differ from REST?
flashcards.back: GraphQL is a query language for APIs that allows clients to request exactly the data they need. Unlike REST, which exposes fixed endpoints, GraphQL uses a single endpoint and a type system to enable flexible, efficient data fetching.

flashcards.front: What is Kubernetes and why is it used?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It provides service discovery, load balancing, self-healing, and rolling updates.

flashcards.front: What is event-driven architecture?
flashcards.back: Event-driven architecture is a design pattern where components communicate by producing and consuming events. It enables loose coupling, scalability, and real-time processing, often using message brokers like Kafka or RabbitMQ.

questions.answer_outline: Strong answers show structured debugging: forming hypotheses, gathering data, isolating variables, and fixing root cause rather than symptoms. Look for ownership, communication during incidents, and follow-up prevention.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a project where you worked closely with product and other engineering teams. How did you handle conflicting priorities or ambiguous requirements?
questions.answer_outline: Look for clear communication, proactive clarification, tradeoff discussions, and shared ownership of outcomes. Candidate should show they can translate product goals into technical plans and push back constructively.

questions.prompt: Do you have experience with e-commerce systems or GraphQL? If so, describe how you've used them and what you learned.
questions.answer_outline: Nice-to-have. Candidate may discuss carts, checkout, inventory, payments, or GraphQL schema design, resolvers, and N+1 issues. If no direct experience, look for adjacent knowledge and genuine interest in learning.

questions.prompt: Have you worked with Kubernetes or event-driven architecture? Describe your experience and how it shaped your approach to building reliable services.
questions.answer_outline: Nice-to-have. Look for container orchestration, deployments, scaling, and observability with K8s; for event-driven, look for message brokers, event schemas, ordering, and idempotent consumers. Adjacent experience is acceptable if the candidate shows curiosity.

flashcards.front: What does '3+ years of backend development experience' typically entail?
flashcards.back: It means you have at least three years of professional experience building and maintaining server-side applications, including designing APIs, working with databases, and deploying to production.

flashcards.front: Which languages are commonly used for backend development in this context?
flashcards.back: Ruby (especially with Rails) and Node.js are explicitly mentioned, but similar backend languages like Python, Java, or Go may also qualify.

flashcards.front: What is a REST API and why is it important?
flashcards.back: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to perform CRUD operations on resources, enabling stateless, scalable communication between clients and servers.

flashcards.front: What are key concepts in SQL and relational databases?
flashcards.back: Key concepts include tables, rows, columns, primary keys, foreign keys, indexes, joins, transactions, ACID properties, and normalization. Proficiency in writing complex queries and optimizing performance is essential.

flashcards.front: What are distributed systems and why are they used?
flashcards.back: Distributed systems are collections of independent computers that appear as a single coherent system to users. They are used for scalability, fault tolerance, and high availability, but introduce challenges like network latency, consistency, and partitioning.

flashcards.front: What considerations are important for high-traffic applications?
flashcards.back: High-traffic applications require scalability (horizontal/vertical), caching, load balancing, database sharding/replication, asynchronous processing, and monitoring to handle large volumes of requests without downtime.

flashcards.front: How can you demonstrate strong problem-solving skills in an interview?
flashcards.back: By walking through your thought process, breaking down complex problems, considering trade-offs, and describing how you've debugged and resolved issues in past projects.

flashcards.front: What does effective collaboration with product and engineering teams involve?
flashcards.back: It involves clear communication, understanding business requirements, providing technical feasibility feedback, participating in agile ceremonies, and aligning engineering efforts with product goals.

flashcards.front: What are common e-commerce backend challenges?
flashcards.back: Challenges include inventory management, payment processing, order fulfillment, scalability during peak traffic, security (PCI compliance), and integrating with third-party services.

flashcards.front: What is GraphQL and how does it differ from REST?
flashcards.back: GraphQL is a query language for APIs that allows clients to request exactly the data they need. Unlike REST, which exposes fixed endpoints, GraphQL uses a single endpoint and a type system to enable flexible, efficient data fetching.

flashcards.front: What is Kubernetes and why is it used?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It provides service discovery, load balancing, self-healing, and rolling updates.

flashcards.front: What is event-driven architecture?
flashcards.back: Event-driven architecture is a design pattern where components communicate by producing and consuming events. It enables loose coupling, scalability, and real-time processing, often using message brokers like Kafka or RabbitMQ.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a software project where you had significant ownership over a complex system. What was your role, what technical challenges did you face, and how did you measure the impact of your work?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate 4+ years of experience by detailing a project with clear ownership, technical depth, and measurable outcomes. Look for specific technologies used, problems solved, and metrics like performance improvements or user growth.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you approach mentoring junior engineers and conducting code reviews? Provide an example of how you've helped a team member grow technically.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should show leadership and experience beyond coding. Look for specific mentoring techniques, constructive feedback, and examples of mentee improvement. This assesses seniority and collaboration.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how you would design a reusable TypeScript React component that fetches data from an API, handles loading and error states, and is easily testable. What patterns or libraries would you use?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss TypeScript generics, custom hooks, state management, and testing strategies. Look for knowledge of React patterns like render props, hooks, and separation of concerns.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the key differences between using `any`, `unknown`, and generics in TypeScript? Provide a scenario where each is appropriate in a React application.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should explain type safety, when to use `any` (rarely), `unknown` for safer alternatives, and generics for reusable components. Look for understanding of TypeScript's type system and best practices.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a backend service that processes and stores user-generated content. What technologies would you choose and why? Discuss scalability, security, and data consistency.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate backend architecture skills, including choice of language/framework, database, caching, and message queues. Look for considerations of load balancing, authentication, and transaction management.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you handle database migrations and schema changes in a production environment with zero downtime?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss strategies like backward-compatible migrations, blue-green deployments, and tools like Flyway or Liquibase. Look for understanding of rollback plans and testing.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a RESTful API for a simple e-commerce application. Define the endpoints, request/response formats, and error handling. How would you version this API?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should outline resource-based endpoints, HTTP methods, status codes, and JSON schemas. Look for versioning strategies (e.g., URL versioning) and consistency in error responses.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the key considerations when designing an API for external developers? Discuss authentication, rate limiting, documentation, and backward compatibility.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover OAuth, API keys, rate limiting strategies, OpenAPI/Swagger docs, and deprecation policies. Look for focus on developer experience and long-term maintenance.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how you would optimize a slow PostgreSQL query. What tools and techniques would you use?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should mention EXPLAIN ANALYZE, indexing strategies, query rewriting, and partitioning. Look for understanding of database internals and performance tuning.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had to design a complex database schema in PostgreSQL. How did you ensure data integrity and performance?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss normalization, constraints, indexes, and possibly denormalization for performance. Look for experience with transactions, foreign keys, and scaling considerations.

initial_questions.prompt: Walk us through a user-facing feature you built from concept to launch. How did you ensure a polished user experience?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should highlight attention to detail, user research, iterative design, and cross-functional collaboration. Look for metrics like user engagement or satisfaction.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you balance technical constraints with user experience requirements when building a product? Provide an example.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate empathy for users and pragmatic decision-making. Look for examples of trade-offs, such as performance vs. features, and how they communicated with stakeholders.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a time when you had to make a significant architectural decision for a system. What factors did you consider, and what was the outcome?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss trade-offs, scalability, maintainability, and alignment with business goals. Look for structured decision-making and lessons learned.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you approach designing a system for high availability and fault tolerance? Discuss patterns like circuit breakers, retries, and redundancy.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate knowledge of distributed systems patterns and resilience engineering. Look for real-world examples and understanding of CAP theorem.

initial_questions.prompt: Have you worked with AI-powered features in a product? Describe how you integrated an AI model (e.g., recommendation, NLP) into an application and the challenges you faced.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss model selection, data pipelines, latency, and user feedback loops. Look for experience with APIs like OpenAI or custom models, and handling of edge cases.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the key considerations when building a product that relies on machine learning models? How do you handle model updates and monitoring?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover versioning, A/B testing, drift detection, and fallback mechanisms. Look for understanding of MLOps and user experience implications.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how GraphQL differs from REST. What are the advantages and disadvantages of using GraphQL in a production application?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss schema, resolvers, over-fetching, and caching. Look for awareness of complexity, performance, and tooling like Apollo.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a GraphQL schema for a social media application. How would you handle authentication, pagination, and real-time updates?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should define types, queries, mutations, and subscriptions. Look for strategies for pagination (cursor-based), auth directives, and subscription implementation.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe how you would implement real-time features like chat or live notifications in a web application. What technologies and protocols would you use?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should mention WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, or polling. Look for understanding of scaling real-time systems, message brokers, and state synchronization.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the challenges of maintaining consistency in a real-time collaborative application (e.g., Google Docs)? How would you address them?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss conflict resolution, operational transforms, CRDTs, and eventual consistency. Look for deep understanding of distributed systems.

initial_questions.prompt: Have you worked at a fast-growing startup? Describe how you adapted to rapid changes, wore multiple hats, and contributed to scaling the product.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate flexibility, ownership, and ability to prioritize. Look for examples of building processes, hiring, and handling ambiguity.

initial_questions.prompt: In a startup environment, how do you balance building new features with maintaining code quality and technical debt? Provide an example.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should show pragmatic decision-making, such as incremental refactoring and automated testing. Look for experience with rapid iteration and avoiding over-engineering.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a time when you had to collaborate with a teammate or stakeholder who had a very different working style or communication preference from yours. How did you adapt to keep the collaboration effective?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Situation: name the project and the difference in style (e.g., detail-oriented vs. big-picture, async vs. synchronous). Task: explain why collaboration was necessary and what was at stake. Action: describe concrete adjustments you made—e.g., switching channels, summarizing decisions in writing, setting shared norms, checking understanding. Result: outcome for the project and relationship, plus what you learned about communicating across styles.

initial_questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when a communication breakdown caused a problem on your team. What did you do to repair it, and what changed afterward?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Situation: describe the breakdown (missed handoff, unclear ownership, conflicting messages). Task: clarify your responsibility in resolving it. Action: explain how you surfaced the issue, facilitated a conversation, aligned on a shared plan, and improved communication (e.g., written updates, clearer roles, regular syncs). Result: resolution, impact on delivery/team trust, and preventive measures.

initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should summarize 4+ years of engineering experience, ideally with concrete examples from startups or fast-paced teams. initial_questions.prompt: Linear's UI is known for being exceptionally polished and fast. Describe a user-facing product you built with TypeScript and React where you obsessed over polish and performance. What specific decisions did you make to achieve that quality?

initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should explain backend architecture, data flow, scaling considerations, and trade-offs. Look for strong software architecture understanding, not just implementation. Bonus if they discuss real-time or collaborative systems.

initial_questions.prompt: Designing APIs and working with PostgreSQL are core to this role. Walk us through an API you designed end-to-end, including the PostgreSQL schema and how you handled versioning, performance, and data integrity.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe API design principles (REST/GraphQL, versioning, error handling) and PostgreSQL specifics (indexing, migrations, transactions, constraints). Look for thoughtful trade-offs and real production experience.

initial_questions.answer_outline: This is a nice-to-have. Candidate should honestly describe any AI product or GraphQL experience, focusing on how it could help Linear. If they lack it, they should show curiosity and ability to learn quickly.

initial_questions.answer_outline: Nice-to-have. Candidate should explain real-time concepts and trade-offs (latency, conflict resolution, offline support). Look for practical experience or a thoughtful approach to designing real-time features.

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 4+ years of software engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight a progression of roles and projects spanning at least four years, focusing on increasing responsibility, complex systems delivered, and measurable impact. Use specific examples like leading a feature from design to production, mentoring junior engineers, and improving system reliability or performance.

flashcards.front: What are key concepts in TypeScript that you use daily with React?
flashcards.back: Generics for reusable components, strict typing for props and state, discriminated unions for state management, utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit), and type guards. In React, use TypeScript to type hooks, event handlers, and context, ensuring type safety across the component tree.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure strong backend development practices?
flashcards.back: Focus on modular architecture, separation of concerns, robust error handling, logging, monitoring, and automated testing (unit, integration). Use design patterns, dependency injection, and adhere to SOLID principles. Optimize database queries, manage transactions, and secure endpoints with authentication/authorization.

flashcards.front: What principles guide your API design?
flashcards.back: RESTful conventions (or GraphQL), clear resource naming, versioning, consistent error responses, pagination, filtering, and HATEOAS when appropriate. Prioritize simplicity, predictability, and documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger). Consider idempotency, rate limiting, and backward compatibility.

flashcards.front: How do you optimize PostgreSQL performance?
flashcards.back: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify slow queries, add appropriate indexes (B-tree, GIN, etc.), avoid N+1 queries with JOINs or batch loading, partition large tables, and tune configuration (work_mem, shared_buffers). Regularly VACUUM and ANALYZE, and use connection pooling.

flashcards.front: What makes a user-facing product 'polished'?
flashcards.back: Attention to detail: smooth animations, responsive design, accessibility (WCAG), consistent design system, fast load times, intuitive navigation, error handling with helpful messages, and delightful micro-interactions. It also involves thorough testing across devices and browsers.

flashcards.front: How do you approach software architecture for a new system?
flashcards.back: Start with requirements and constraints, then choose appropriate patterns (microservices, monolith, event-driven). Consider scalability, maintainability, and team structure. Document decisions with ADRs, define clear boundaries, and plan for observability, security, and deployment.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure effective communication and collaboration in a team?
flashcards.back: Use clear written and verbal communication, active listening, and empathy. Participate in code reviews, pair programming, and knowledge sharing. Document decisions, provide constructive feedback, and align with stakeholders through regular syncs and transparent updates.

flashcards.front: What experience do you have with AI-powered products?
flashcards.back: Integrating ML models via APIs (e.g., OpenAI, Hugging Face), building features like recommendations, chatbots, or image recognition. Handling data pipelines, model deployment, monitoring performance, and ensuring ethical AI use. Collaborating with data scientists to productionize models.

flashcards.front: How do you design a GraphQL schema?
flashcards.back: Define types and fields based on client needs, use interfaces and unions for polymorphism, implement pagination with connections, and avoid overly nested queries. Use resolvers efficiently, batch with DataLoader, and secure with depth limiting and query complexity analysis.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations for real-time systems?
flashcards.back: Low latency, high throughput, and reliability. Use WebSockets, SSE, or long polling. Handle reconnection, message ordering, and backpressure. Choose appropriate data stores (e.g., Redis, Kafka) and design for horizontal scaling and fault tolerance.

flashcards.front: What is unique about working at a fast-growing startup?
flashcards.back: High autonomy, rapid iteration, wearing multiple hats, and adapting to changing priorities. Focus on shipping quickly, measuring impact, and scaling systems. Embrace ambiguity, take ownership, and contribute to culture and processes.

questions.prompt: Describe a time when you had to make a significant architectural decision for a system. What factors did you consider, and what was the outcome?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss trade-offs, scalability, maintainability, and alignment with business goals. Look for structured decision-making and lessons learned.

questions.prompt: How do you approach designing a system for high availability and fault tolerance? Discuss patterns like circuit breakers, retries, and redundancy.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate knowledge of distributed systems patterns and resilience engineering. Look for real-world examples and understanding of CAP theorem.

questions.prompt: Have you worked with AI-powered features in a product? Describe how you integrated an AI model (e.g., recommendation, NLP) into an application and the challenges you faced.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss model selection, data pipelines, latency, and user feedback loops. Look for experience with APIs like OpenAI or custom models, and handling of edge cases.

questions.prompt: What are the key considerations when building a product that relies on machine learning models? How do you handle model updates and monitoring?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover versioning, A/B testing, drift detection, and fallback mechanisms. Look for understanding of MLOps and user experience implications.

questions.prompt: Explain how GraphQL differs from REST. What are the advantages and disadvantages of using GraphQL in a production application?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss schema, resolvers, over-fetching, and caching. Look for awareness of complexity, performance, and tooling like Apollo.

questions.prompt: Design a GraphQL schema for a social media application. How would you handle authentication, pagination, and real-time updates?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should define types, queries, mutations, and subscriptions. Look for strategies for pagination (cursor-based), auth directives, and subscription implementation.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would implement real-time features like chat or live notifications in a web application. What technologies and protocols would you use?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should mention WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, or polling. Look for understanding of scaling real-time systems, message brokers, and state synchronization.

questions.prompt: What are the challenges of maintaining consistency in a real-time collaborative application (e.g., Google Docs)? How would you address them?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss conflict resolution, operational transforms, CRDTs, and eventual consistency. Look for deep understanding of distributed systems.

questions.prompt: Have you worked at a fast-growing startup? Describe how you adapted to rapid changes, wore multiple hats, and contributed to scaling the product.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate flexibility, ownership, and ability to prioritize. Look for examples of building processes, hiring, and handling ambiguity.

questions.prompt: In a startup environment, how do you balance building new features with maintaining code quality and technical debt? Provide an example.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should show pragmatic decision-making, such as incremental refactoring and automated testing. Look for experience with rapid iteration and avoiding over-engineering.

questions.prompt: Describe a time when you had to collaborate with a teammate or stakeholder who had a very different working style or communication preference from yours. How did you adapt to keep the collaboration effective?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: name the project and the difference in style (e.g., detail-oriented vs. big-picture, async vs. synchronous). Task: explain why collaboration was necessary and what was at stake. Action: describe concrete adjustments you made—e.g., switching channels, summarizing decisions in writing, setting shared norms, checking understanding. Result: outcome for the project and relationship, plus what you learned about communicating across styles.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when a communication breakdown caused a problem on your team. What did you do to repair it, and what changed afterward?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: describe the breakdown (missed handoff, unclear ownership, conflicting messages). Task: clarify your responsibility in resolving it. Action: explain how you surfaced the issue, facilitated a conversation, aligned on a shared plan, and improved communication (e.g., written updates, clearer roles, regular syncs). Result: resolution, impact on delivery/team trust, and preventive measures.

questions.prompt: Linear is a fast-moving product company building for teams and agents. Walk us through your 4+ years of software engineering experience and highlight any time you worked in a fast-growing startup environment. What did you learn about shipping quickly without breaking quality?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should summarize 4+ years of engineering experience, ideally with concrete examples from startups or fast-paced teams. Look for evidence of ownership, rapid iteration, and balancing speed with reliability. Strong answers connect startup experience to Linear's pace and product focus.

questions.prompt: Linear's UI is known for being exceptionally polished and fast. Describe a user-facing product you built with TypeScript and React where you obsessed over polish and performance. What specific decisions did you make to achieve that quality?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe a real product, the TypeScript/React architecture used, and concrete polish/performance techniques (e.g., optimistic UI, rendering strategy, accessibility, design collaboration). Look for pride in craft and attention to detail aligned with Linear's brand.

questions.prompt: Linear's product spans a complex backend and real-time collaboration. Tell us about a backend system you designed or significantly contributed to. What architectural trade-offs did you make, and how did you ensure it could scale?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should explain backend architecture, data flow, scaling considerations, and trade-offs. Look for strong software architecture understanding, not just implementation. Bonus if they discuss real-time or collaborative systems.

questions.prompt: Designing APIs and working with PostgreSQL are core to this role. Walk us through an API you designed end-to-end, including the PostgreSQL schema and how you handled versioning, performance, and data integrity.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe API design principles (REST/GraphQL, versioning, error handling) and PostgreSQL specifics (indexing, migrations, transactions, constraints). Look for thoughtful trade-offs and real production experience.

questions.prompt: Linear is a highly collaborative, product-driven company. Give an example of a time you had to communicate a complex technical decision to non-engineers or align a cross-functional team. How did you approach it?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate clear communication, empathy for different audiences, and collaboration. Look for structured storytelling, listening skills, and outcomes that show alignment across design, product, and engineering.

questions.prompt: Linear is building for the AI era, with features like Agent Insights and Triage Intelligence. Have you worked with AI-powered products or GraphQL? If so, describe your experience and how it might apply to Linear's direction.
questions.answer_outline: This is a nice-to-have. Candidate should honestly describe any AI product or GraphQL experience, focusing on how it could help Linear. If they lack it, they should show curiosity and ability to learn quickly.

questions.prompt: Linear's product relies on real-time collaboration and fast sync. Describe any experience you have with real-time systems (e.g., WebSockets, CRDTs, sync engines). How would you approach building a real-time feature at Linear?
questions.answer_outline: Nice-to-have. Candidate should explain real-time concepts and trade-offs (latency, conflict resolution, offline support). Look for practical experience or a thoughtful approach to designing real-time features.

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 4+ years of software engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight a progression of roles and projects spanning at least four years, focusing on increasing responsibility, complex systems delivered, and measurable impact. Use specific examples like leading a feature from design to production, mentoring junior engineers, and improving system reliability or performance.

flashcards.front: What are key concepts in TypeScript that you use daily with React?
flashcards.back: Generics for reusable components, strict typing for props and state, discriminated unions for state management, utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit), and type guards. In React, use TypeScript to type hooks, event handlers, and context, ensuring type safety across the component tree.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure strong backend development practices?
flashcards.back: Focus on modular architecture, separation of concerns, robust error handling, logging, monitoring, and automated testing (unit, integration). Use design patterns, dependency injection, and adhere to SOLID principles. Optimize database queries, manage transactions, and secure endpoints with authentication/authorization.

flashcards.front: What principles guide your API design?
flashcards.back: RESTful conventions (or GraphQL), clear resource naming, versioning, consistent error responses, pagination, filtering, and HATEOAS when appropriate. Prioritize simplicity, predictability, and documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger). Consider idempotency, rate limiting, and backward compatibility.

flashcards.front: How do you optimize PostgreSQL performance?
flashcards.back: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify slow queries, add appropriate indexes (B-tree, GIN, etc.), avoid N+1 queries with JOINs or batch loading, partition large tables, and tune configuration (work_mem, shared_buffers). Regularly VACUUM and ANALYZE, and use connection pooling.

flashcards.front: What makes a user-facing product 'polished'?
flashcards.back: Attention to detail: smooth animations, responsive design, accessibility (WCAG), consistent design system, fast load times, intuitive navigation, error handling with helpful messages, and delightful micro-interactions. It also involves thorough testing across devices and browsers.

flashcards.front: How do you approach software architecture for a new system?
flashcards.back: Start with requirements and constraints, then choose appropriate patterns (microservices, monolith, event-driven). Consider scalability, maintainability, and team structure. Document decisions with ADRs, define clear boundaries, and plan for observability, security, and deployment.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure effective communication and collaboration in a team?
flashcards.back: Use clear written and verbal communication, active listening, and empathy. Participate in code reviews, pair programming, and knowledge sharing. Document decisions, provide constructive feedback, and align with stakeholders through regular syncs and transparent updates.

flashcards.front: What experience do you have with AI-powered products?
flashcards.back: Integrating ML models via APIs (e.g., OpenAI, Hugging Face), building features like recommendations, chatbots, or image recognition. Handling data pipelines, model deployment, monitoring performance, and ensuring ethical AI use. Collaborating with data scientists to productionize models.

flashcards.front: How do you design a GraphQL schema?
flashcards.back: Define types and fields based on client needs, use interfaces and unions for polymorphism, implement pagination with connections, and avoid overly nested queries. Use resolvers efficiently, batch with DataLoader, and secure with depth limiting and query complexity analysis.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations for real-time systems?
flashcards.back: Low latency, high throughput, and reliability. Use WebSockets, SSE, or long polling. Handle reconnection, message ordering, and backpressure. Choose appropriate data stores (e.g., Redis, Kafka) and design for horizontal scaling and fault tolerance.

flashcards.front: What is unique about working at a fast-growing startup?
flashcards.back: High autonomy, rapid iteration, wearing multiple hats, and adapting to changing priorities. Focus on shipping quickly, measuring impact, and scaling systems. Embrace ambiguity, take ownership, and contribute to culture and processes.

If you’re reading this, you’re probably like me—spending most of your days in your office, in front of a computer.You probably have fifteen tabs open: one for email, one for Slack, one for Google Docs, and on, and on…But have you ever thought about where these “work tools” came from? Or why there are so many of them?To answer these questions, and to explain why we created Notion, we have to travel back in time.As people flooded to factories during the Industrial Revolution, many tools were invented to ease the management overload.Typewriters replaced illegible handwriting. File cabinets stored more information than any clerk could remember (and also won the gold medal at the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair!)Tools like these paved the way for offices as we know them today.Fast forward to the 1950s, when computers came into the workplace.At first, they were lifeless, room-sized monsters that operated on paper and punch cards. initial_questions.prompt: Explain how TypeScript's structural typing and generics can be used to create a type-safe API client. Provide an example with conditional types or mapped types.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the differences between `interface` and `type` in TypeScript? When would you use each, and how do they affect declaration merging and performance?

flashcards.front: How can you demonstrate 3+ years of software engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight specific projects and roles where you delivered production software over multiple years. Discuss the evolution of your responsibilities, technologies used, and impact on business metrics. Quantify achievements and show a progression of skills.

flashcards.front: What are key TypeScript features you should be prepared to discuss?
flashcards.back: Generics, interfaces, type guards, union/intersection types, decorators, async/await with Promises, and advanced types like conditional and mapped types. Be ready to explain how they improve code safety and maintainability.

flashcards.front: How do you approach building an AI-powered application?
flashcards.back: Start by defining the problem and success metrics. Choose appropriate models (e.g., LLMs) and integrate via APIs. Design for scalability, handle errors, and monitor performance. Iterate based on user feedback and data.

flashcards.front: What considerations are important when designing APIs for distributed services?
flashcards.back: Idempotency, versioning, rate limiting, authentication/authorization, error handling, and observability. Use REST or GraphQL appropriately, and ensure services communicate reliably via message queues or gRPC.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure efficient database interactions in a high-load application?
flashcards.back: Use indexing, query optimization, caching, connection pooling, and read replicas. Choose the right database (SQL vs NoSQL) based on access patterns. Monitor slow queries and scale horizontally when needed.

flashcards.front: Describe your debugging process for a complex production issue.
flashcards.back: Reproduce the issue, gather logs and metrics, form hypotheses, and isolate variables. Use tools like debuggers, profilers, and tracing. Implement a fix, add tests, and document root cause to prevent recurrence.

flashcards.front: Give an example of working cross-functionally to deliver a feature.
flashcards.back: Collaborated with product, design, and QA to define requirements, estimate effort, and align on timelines. Held regular syncs, addressed dependencies, and ensured smooth handoffs. Resulted in on-time delivery and positive user feedback.

flashcards.front: How do you tailor communication for technical and non-technical audiences?
flashcards.back: For technical audiences, use precise terminology and dive into implementation details. For non-technical, focus on business impact, analogies, and avoid jargon. Always confirm understanding and encourage questions.

flashcards.front: What are best practices for integrating LLMs into applications?
flashcards.back: Use prompt engineering, manage token limits, handle rate limits and costs, implement fallbacks, and ensure data privacy. Consider fine-tuning or few-shot learning for specific tasks. Monitor output quality and bias.

flashcards.front: Explain the architecture of a RAG system you have built.
flashcards.back: Components: document ingestion, chunking, embedding generation, vector database, retrieval, and LLM generation. Use similarity search to fetch relevant chunks, then augment the prompt. Evaluate retrieval accuracy and generation relevance.

flashcards.front: How do you design an agentic system that can autonomously perform tasks?
flashcards.back: Define goals, tools, and constraints. Use planning (e.g., ReAct, chain-of-thought), memory, and tool invocation. Implement safety checks, error recovery, and human-in-the-loop for critical decisions. Test in sandboxed environments.

flashcards.front: What React concepts are essential for building performant UIs?
flashcards.back: Component lifecycle, hooks (useState, useEffect, useContext), memoization (React.memo, useMemo, useCallback), code splitting, and state management (Redux, Context). Understand reconciliation and virtual DOM.

flashcards.front: How can you demonstrate 3+ years of software engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight specific projects and roles where you delivered production software over multiple years. Discuss the evolution of your responsibilities, technologies used, and impact on business metrics. Quantify achievements and show a progression of skills.

flashcards.front: What are key TypeScript features you should be prepared to discuss?
flashcards.back: Generics, interfaces, type guards, union/intersection types, decorators, async/await with Promises, and advanced types like conditional and mapped types. Be ready to explain how they improve code safety and maintainability.

flashcards.front: How do you approach building an AI-powered application?
flashcards.back: Start by defining the problem and success metrics. Choose appropriate models (e.g., LLMs) and integrate via APIs. Design for scalability, handle errors, and monitor performance. Iterate based on user feedback and data.

flashcards.front: What considerations are important when designing APIs for distributed services?
flashcards.back: Idempotency, versioning, rate limiting, authentication/authorization, error handling, and observability. Use REST or GraphQL appropriately, and ensure services communicate reliably via message queues or gRPC.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure efficient database interactions in a high-load application?
flashcards.back: Use indexing, query optimization, caching, connection pooling, and read replicas. Choose the right database (SQL vs NoSQL) based on access patterns. Monitor slow queries and scale horizontally when needed.

flashcards.front: Describe your debugging process for a complex production issue.
flashcards.back: Reproduce the issue, gather logs and metrics, form hypotheses, and isolate variables. Use tools like debuggers, profilers, and tracing. Implement a fix, add tests, and document root cause to prevent recurrence.

flashcards.front: Give an example of working cross-functionally to deliver a feature.
flashcards.back: Collaborated with product, design, and QA to define requirements, estimate effort, and align on timelines. Held regular syncs, addressed dependencies, and ensured smooth handoffs. Resulted in on-time delivery and positive user feedback.

flashcards.front: How do you tailor communication for technical and non-technical audiences?
flashcards.back: For technical audiences, use precise terminology and dive into implementation details. For non-technical, focus on business impact, analogies, and avoid jargon. Always confirm understanding and encourage questions.

flashcards.front: What are best practices for integrating LLMs into applications?
flashcards.back: Use prompt engineering, manage token limits, handle rate limits and costs, implement fallbacks, and ensure data privacy. Consider fine-tuning or few-shot learning for specific tasks. Monitor output quality and bias.

flashcards.front: Explain the architecture of a RAG system you have built.
flashcards.back: Components: document ingestion, chunking, embedding generation, vector database, retrieval, and LLM generation. Use similarity search to fetch relevant chunks, then augment the prompt. Evaluate retrieval accuracy and generation relevance.

flashcards.front: How do you design an agentic system that can autonomously perform tasks?
flashcards.back: Define goals, tools, and constraints. Use planning (e.g., ReAct, chain-of-thought), memory, and tool invocation. Implement safety checks, error recovery, and human-in-the-loop for critical decisions. Test in sandboxed environments.

flashcards.front: What React concepts are essential for building performant UIs?
flashcards.back: Component lifecycle, hooks (useState, useEffect, useContext), memoization (React.memo, useMemo, useCallback), code splitting, and state management (Redux, Context). Understand reconciliation and virtual DOM.
